## CAP/DA General Eligibility Criteria Under NC Medicaid

The **Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)** is a Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) Medicaid waiver program. The governing policy is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2**. No amendments were found, so the base policy is current.

---

### 1. 📋 Medicaid Enrollment Requirements
*(Policy 3K-2, Section 2.1.2a — "a. Medicaid")*

To be eligible, a beneficiary must:

- Be **enrolled in fee-for-service Medicaid (Medicaid Direct)**
- Be **determined to require a level of institutional care** under the NC State Medicaid Plan
- Be a **member of a target group** documented in the approved waiver application
- Meet applicable **Medicaid eligibility criteria** (see Section 2.1.2b)
- **Exercise freedom of choice** by voluntarily choosing to enter or remain in the waiver
- Be **assigned a CAP/DA waiver slot**
- Be able to have their **health, safety, and well-being maintained** at their primary residence or an approved location using both formal and informal supports
- Be **age 18 years old or older**

---

### 2. 🏥 Medicaid Eligibility Category
*(Policy 3K-2, Section 2.1.2b — "b. Medicaid Eligibility Requirements")*

The beneficiary must be enrolled under one of the following Medicaid categories:

- **Medicaid to the Aged (MAA)**
- **Medicaid to the Blind (MAB)**
- **Medicaid to the Disabled (MAD)**
- **Health Care for Workers with Disabilities (HCWD)**

---

### 3. ✅ Specific Coverage Criteria
*(Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1)*

Medicaid covers CAP/DA when the beneficiary meets **all** of the following:

1. **Nursing Facility Level of Care (LOC):** Meets the required HCBS nursing facility level of care as determined by NC Medicaid, requiring long-term care support typically provided in an institution, directly related to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need — **assessed quarterly**.

2. **Reasonable Indication of Need:** The completed CAP assessment finds a reasonable indication that the individual would need at least one CAP/DA HCBS service within **30 calendar days** of evaluation.

3. **Signed Service Plan:** Must have a signed service plan authorizing one or more waiver services on a **monthly basis** to mitigate institutionalization through coordinated case management.

4. **Equipment/Modification Plan (if applicable):** A signed service plan authorizing installation of equipment, modification, or technology to allow the person to remain in their primary private residence — installation must be completed within **3 calendar months** of service plan approval.

5. **Health, Safety & Well-Being:** Able to maintain health, safety, and well-being at their **primary private residence** or an approved location with formal and informal supports.

6. **Cost Effectiveness:** Paid care needs can be **maintained within the average institutional cost** of the CAP/DA waiver.

7. **Primary Physician:** Must have a primary physician who can link and coordinate all medical services.

8. **Emergency Back-Up Plan:** Must have an emergency back-up and disaster plan specifying who will provide care when key direct care staff are unavailable or during a public health emergency.

---

### 4. 🩺 Qualifying Medical Conditions (Level of Care)
*(Policy 3K-2, Section 3.1a — "a. Qualifying Conditions")*

The nursing facility level of care may be established based on medical need, including conditions such as:

- Need for **RN/LPN supervision** or observation for acute episodes or changes in treatment
- **Restorative nursing measures** (e.g., ADL assistance, range of motion, ambulation training)
- **Dialysis** (hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis)
- **Specialized therapeutic diet** (physician-prescribed)
- **Medication administration** requiring a licensed nurse (e.g., IV drugs, frequent injections)
- **Nasogastric or gastrostomy feedings**
- **Respiratory therapy** (oxygen, nebulizer, suctioning)
- **Wound care** (decubitus ulcers or open areas)
- **Rehabilitative services** by a licensed therapist

Additionally, HCBS nursing facility LOC may be established with **two or more Category I conditions**, or **one or more from both Category I and Category II**:

- **Category I examples:** Chronic recurrent medical problems, blindness, diabetes requiring daily observation, frequent falls, behavioral problems due to cognitive impairment
- **Category II examples:** Need for teaching/counseling related to disease or diet, adaptive re-training programs, acute psychological symptoms, age and social support factors

---

### 5. 🔄 Consumer-Directed Services (CAP/CD)
*(Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1)*

Beneficiaries who meet all of the above criteria may also qualify for **consumer-directed services** if they:
- Understand the rights and responsibilities of directing their own care (evidenced by a mandatory self-assessment questionnaire and introductory training)
- Are willing and emotionally capable of assuming employer responsibilities, or select a representative to do so

---

### Key Takeaways

| Criterion | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Age** | 18 years or older |
| **Medicaid type** | Fee-for-service (Medicaid Direct) |
| **Medicaid category** | MAA, MAB, MAD, or HCWD |
| **Level of care** | Nursing facility level of care |
| **Setting** | Primary private residence or approved location |
| **Cost** | Within average institutional cost |
| **Waiver slot** | Must be assigned one |

> **Source:** NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy **3K-2** (Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults). No amendments on file. For the most current information, verify with NC DHHS or the CAP/DA Case Management Entity (CME).

# NC Medicaid: Outpatient Behavioral Health Services — Coverage Criteria
**Source: Clinical Coverage Policy 8C — *Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers***
*(No amendments on file; base policy is current as retrieved.)*

These criteria appear under **Section 3.0 – When the Procedure, Product, or Service Is Covered → Section 3.2.1 – Specific Criteria Covered by Medicaid.**

---

## 1. 🚪 Entrance Criteria
*(Section 3.2.1.1)*

A beneficiary must meet **all** of the following to begin outpatient behavioral health services:

1. **Current DSM-5 diagnosis** — The beneficiary must have a current diagnosis under the *Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition* (DSM-5), or any subsequent edition.

2. **Functional impairment** — The beneficiary presents behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment that are consistent with and associated with the current diagnosis.

3. **Higher level of care unavailable or refused** — If a higher level of care is clinically indicated but is unavailable, or the beneficiary is refusing it, outpatient services may be provided until the appropriate level of care becomes available or to support the beneficiary in participating in that higher level of care.

4. **Capacity to benefit** — The beneficiary is capable of developing skills to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions.

5. **No more effective alternative** — There is no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective, based on North Carolina community practice standards (including Best Practice Guidelines of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, American Psychiatric Association, and American Board of Addiction Medicine).

---

## 2. 🔄 Continued Service Criteria
*(Section 3.2.1.2)*

To continue receiving services, the beneficiary must meet **one criterion from Group A AND one criterion from Group B**:

### Group A — Any ONE of the following:
- The desired outcome or level of functioning has **not been restored, improved, or sustained** over the timeframe outlined in the treatment plan; **OR**
- The beneficiary **continues to be at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; **OR**
- The **tenuous nature of functional gains** warrants continued support.

### Group B — Any ONE of the following (in addition to Group A):
- The beneficiary has **achieved current treatment plan goals**, and additional goals are indicated as evidenced by documented symptoms; **OR**
- The beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress** toward meeting goals, with documentation to support that progress.

---

## 3. 🏁 Discharge Criteria
*(Section 3.2.1.3)*

Discharge is appropriate when **any one** of the following applies:

1. **Functional improvement** — The beneficiary's level of functioning has improved with respect to the goals outlined in the treatment plan.

2. **Voluntary withdrawal** — The beneficiary or legally responsible person no longer wishes to receive these services.

3. **Need for different treatment modality** — Based on the beneficiary's presentation and failure to show improvement despite modifications to the treatment plan, a more appropriate best-practice or evidence-based treatment modality is required, consistent with North Carolina community practice standards (National Institute of Drug Abuse, American Psychiatric Association).

---

## Key Takeaways for Practitioners and Advocates

| Stage | Standard | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| **Entrance** | All 5 criteria must be met | Conjunctive (AND) |
| **Continued Service** | 1 from Group A + 1 from Group B | Two-part conjunctive |
| **Discharge** | Any 1 criterion | Disjunctive (OR) |

- **Treatment plan alignment** is central to all three stages — goals must be documented and updated.
- **Higher level of care** situations are explicitly accommodated at entrance: a beneficiary who needs but cannot access (or refuses) a higher level of care can still receive outpatient services.
- **Discharge is not punitive** — it can occur due to improvement, voluntary choice, or clinical redirection to a better-fit modality.

> ⚠️ **Note:** This policy applies to **direct-enrolled providers** in NC Medicaid. Beneficiaries enrolled in **NC Medicaid Managed Care (PHPs)** should verify whether their health plan applies the same or additional criteria. Always confirm the current version of Policy 8C with DHHS if high-stakes decisions are involved.

## EPSDT Special Provision & Ordering Practitioner Requirements for Outpatient Therapy — Beneficiaries Under 21

**Governing Policy:** Clinical Coverage Policy 10A — *Outpatient Specialized Therapies*
**Effective Date:** February 1, 2025
**No amendments on file** (confirmed via amendment check)

---

### 1. What Services Are Covered Under Policy 10A

Clinical Coverage Policy 10A governs the following **outpatient specialized therapies** (Section 1.0):
- Physical Therapy (PT)
- Occupational Therapy (OT)
- Speech-Language Therapy (ST)
- Respiratory Therapy (RT)
- Audiology Therapy

---

### 2. The EPSDT Special Provision (Section 2.2.1)

**Section 2.2.1** is titled *"EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age"* and is grounded in federal law — **42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [Section 1905(r) of the Social Security Act]**.

Under EPSDT, NC Medicaid **must cover services for beneficiaries under 21** that are medically necessary, even if those services would otherwise be subject to policy limitations. However, the EPSDT provision does **not** override coverage exclusions for services that are:
- **Unsafe, ineffective, or experimental/investigational**, or
- **Not medical in nature** or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.

> **Key practical effect:** A child or adolescent under 21 may receive outpatient therapy services beyond the standard visit caps that apply to adults (21+), provided the additional visits are medically necessary. The EPSDT provision essentially lifts the hard annual visit limits that apply to adults, replacing them with individualized medical necessity determinations.

---

### 3. How Visit Limits Differ: Under 21 vs. 21 and Older

This contrast illustrates the EPSDT provision's real-world impact:

#### Adults (21+) — Hard Annual Caps (Section 5.3)
| Service | Annual Visit Limit |
|---|---|
| PT + OT Habilitative (combined) | 30 visits/calendar year |
| PT + OT Rehabilitative (combined) | 30 visits/calendar year |
| Speech Therapy Habilitative | 30 visits/calendar year |
| Speech Therapy Rehabilitative | 30 visits/calendar year |

#### Beneficiaries Under 21 — Medical Necessity Guidelines (Section 5.4)
Rather than hard caps, under-21 beneficiaries are governed by **medical necessity visit guidelines** tied to severity of impairment, within authorization periods:

**Speech-Language & Audiology Therapy (Section 5.4.2):**
| Severity Level | Range of Visits (per authorization period) |
|---|---|
| Mild Impairment | 6 to 26 visits |
| Moderate Impairment | Up to 46 visits |
| Severe Impairment | Up to 52 visits |

- Authorization periods **cannot exceed six calendar months**
- Audiology: 30–60 minute sessions, 1–3 times per week, in 6-month increments; length and duration determined by severity and rate of change

> **Note:** Sections 5.4.1 (Physical and Occupational Therapy) and 5.4.3 (Respiratory Therapy) are listed in the policy structure but returned no additional text in the retrieved content. The framework of severity-based medical necessity guidelines likely applies similarly to PT/OT and RT for under-21 beneficiaries.

---

### 4. EPSDT Does NOT Eliminate Prior Approval (Section b — EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements)

This is a critical point:

> *"If the service, product, or procedure requires prior approval, the fact that the beneficiary is under 21 years of age does **NOT** eliminate the requirement for prior approval."*

Even when EPSDT expands coverage beyond standard policy limits, **prior authorization must still be obtained** if the service requires it. Additional guidance is available in the NCTracks Provider Claims and Billing Assistance Guide and on the EPSDT provider page.

---

### 5. Ordering Practitioner Requirements (Section 3.1.2)

For outpatient therapy services to be covered under Policy 10A, the services must be **ordered by an eligible practitioner**. The following practitioners are authorized to order outpatient specialized therapies:

1. **Medical Doctor (MD)**
2. **Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)**
3. **Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)**
4. **Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)**
5. **Physician Assistant (PA)**
6. **Nurse Practitioner (NP)**

> These ordering requirements apply to **all beneficiaries**, including those under 21. The EPSDT provision expands *what* can be covered and *how much*, but does not waive the requirement that services be ordered by one of these qualified practitioners.

---

### 6. General Medical Necessity Criteria (Section 3.1)

All covered therapy services — regardless of age — must meet these general criteria:
- The service is **individualized, specific, and consistent** with the beneficiary's symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and not in excess of their needs
- The service can be **safely furnished**, and no equally effective, more conservative, or less costly treatment is available statewide
- The service is **not furnished primarily for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider

---

### Summary

| Issue | Rule |
|---|---|
| **EPSDT coverage expansion** | Beneficiaries under 21 may exceed standard visit limits if medically necessary (§ 2.2.1) |
| **EPSDT exclusions** | Does not cover unsafe, experimental, or non-medical services |
| **Prior approval** | Still required even for EPSDT-expanded services |
| **Visit limits (under 21)** | Severity-based guidelines, not hard caps; authorization periods ≤ 6 months |
| **Visit limits (21+)** | Hard cap of 30 visits/year per therapy category |
| **Ordering practitioners** | MD, DO, DPM, CNM, PA, or NP required for all ages |

**Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, Sections 2.2.1, 3.1.2, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, 5.4.2 (effective Feb. 1, 2025). No amendments currently on file.

> ⚠️ **Recommendation:** Given the stakes for pediatric beneficiaries, always verify the current version of Policy 10A directly with NC DHHS or via the NCTracks portal, as clinical policies are updated periodically.

# NC Medicaid Coverage of Personal Care Services (PCS) in Assisted Living Facilities

## Short Answer: **Yes — but under a separate, specific policy**

NC Medicaid does cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries living in certain assisted living and congregate settings, but this coverage is governed by a **separate clinical coverage policy** from standard in-home PCS. There are two distinct PCS policies:

| Policy | Title | Setting |
|---|---|---|
| **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L** | State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) | **Private residences / in-home** |
| **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1** | State Plan PCS Provided in **Congregate Settings** | **Adult Care Homes, group homes, and similar licensed facilities** |

---

## Policy 3L: Standard PCS — Does NOT Cover Assisted Living

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L, Section 3.2.1**, a beneficiary must **reside in a private living arrangement (primary private residence)** to qualify. Furthermore, Section 4.2.1 explicitly states that PCS is not covered when:

> *"the PCS is provided at a location other than the beneficiary's primary private residence, except when EPSDT requirements are met."*

So standard PCS under Policy 3L is **not available** to residents of assisted living or congregate facilities.

---

## Policy 3L-1: Congregate Setting PCS — **Does Cover Assisted Living**

**Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1** specifically governs PCS in congregate settings. To qualify, a beneficiary must meet **all** of the following criteria (Section 3.2.1):

### ✅ Functional/Medical Criteria
The beneficiary must have a medical or mental condition, disability, or cognitive impairment and demonstrate unmet needs for **at least one** of:
- Three of the five qualifying ADLs with limited hands-on assistance;
- Two ADLs, one of which requires extensive assistance; or
- Two ADLs, one of which requires assistance at the full dependence level.

### ✅ Eligible Facility Types
The beneficiary must reside in:
- An **Adult Care Home (ACH)** licensed under NC G.S. §131D-2.1; or
- A **combination home** as defined in NC G.S. §131E-101; or
- A **group home** licensed under Chapter 122C and 10A NCAC 27G .5601(b)(2) as a supervised living facility for two or more adults whose primary diagnosis is mental illness, a developmental disability, or substance abuse dependency.

> ⚠️ **Note:** Not all facilities commonly called "assisted living" are Adult Care Homes under NC law. The facility must hold the specific license type listed above.

### ✅ Additional Required Criteria
- The congregate setting is safe and free of health hazards (as determined by a facility environmental assessment by NC Medicaid or a DHHS-designated contractor);
- The facility has received an inspection by the Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR);
- No other third-party payer is responsible for covering PCS;
- No family/household member or informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the services;
- The required PCS are directly linked to a documented medical or mental condition;
- The beneficiary is under the ongoing direct care of a physician; and
- The beneficiary is **medically stable** and does not require continuous care or monitoring by a licensed nurse.

---

## What Services Are Covered (Section 3.3)

Medicaid covers the following PCS in congregate settings (occurring at minimum once per week):
- Hands-on assistance with qualifying ADLs
- Set-up, supervision, cueing, prompting, and guiding as part of ADL assistance
- Assistance with home management IADLs **directly related** to qualifying ADLs
- Medication assistance linked to a documented medical condition

## CAP/DA Beneficiary Transfers: Rules and Procedures

**Source:** Clinical Coverage Policy No. 3K-2 — *Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)*, effective September 1, 2025. No amendments were found on file.

---

### ✅ Yes — Transfers Are Permitted

CAP/DA beneficiaries **can** transfer between service providers and between counties. The policy establishes specific rules for three distinct transfer scenarios, all governed by **Section 3.3 – Transfers of Eligible Beneficiaries**.

---

### 📋 General Transfer Requirements (All Transfers)

Before **any** transfer takes place, the **Case Management Entity (CME)** must coordinate the transfer to prevent gaps in service. The following steps are **mandatory prior to the transfer**:

1. **Determine the anticipated start date** of service with the new provider.
2. **Coordinate a transition plan** between the outgoing and receiving provider agencies.
3. **Discuss and plan for the health, safety, and well-being** of the beneficiary.
4. **Initiate the transfer of electronic health records** in the CAP Business System (e-CAP/DA) to the receiving county.
5. **Arrange a home visit within five (5) business days** of the date the beneficiary moves to their new primary residence — conducted by the receiving entity — to assess the home environment, identify health and welfare concerns, and plan for mitigation and safety.
6. **Coordinate and plan the provision of services** to start on the **first date of the transfer**.

> *Citation: Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.3*

---

### 🏠 Transfer to a Different County

When a CAP/DA beneficiary moves to a **different county**, the following specific rules apply:

- The **CME designee of the transferring agency** must coordinate the transfer with the **CME designee of the receiving agency** upon the agreed-upon transfer date, or **within 30 calendar days** of the request to transfer.
- Both the transferring and receiving CME designees must **discuss and plan for the health, safety, and well-being** of the beneficiary.
- The **electronic health record is transferred** to the receiving county.
- The receiving CME designee must **arrange a home visit within five (5) business days** of the beneficiary moving into their new primary residence to assess the environment, identify health and welfare concerns, and plan for mitigation and safety.
- The receiving CME designee must **coordinate and plan the provision of services to start on the first date of the transfer** into the receiving county.

> *Citation: Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.3*

---

### 👶 Special Rule: CAP/C Beneficiaries Aging Out and Transferring to CAP/DA

For a **CAP/C beneficiary aging out** (turning 21) who wishes to transfer to CAP/DA, a detailed transition timeline applies:

| Timeframe | Required Action |
|---|---|
| **12 months before birth month** | CAP/C CME designee implements a transition/transfer plan |
| **Age 20 annual needs review** | Completion of a transition plan during the annual assessment |
| **Ongoing** | Consultation with beneficiary and primary caregiver about Medicaid and community resources available after age 21 |
| **90 calendar days before birth month** | A **multidisciplinary team meeting** must be convened to discuss care needs and confirm formal/informal resources can meet those needs |
| **Month before birth month** | Local DSS must be notified to change the CAP evidence code for CAP/DA participation for the identified effective start date |
| **First day of birth month** | CAP/DA services are authorized and provided |

> *Citation: Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.3*

---

### ⭐ Priority Status for Transferring Beneficiaries

Transferring beneficiaries receive **priority consideration** for CAP/DA participation slots. The following groups are explicitly listed as priority:

- **An eligible CAP/DA beneficiary who is transferring to another county or CME**
- **Age 18–20 transitioning from CAP/C**
- A previously eligible CAP/DA or consumer-directed beneficiary transitioning from a short-term rehabilitation placement within **90 calendar days** of placement

> *Citation: Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.4*

---

### ⚠️ Disenrollment vs. Transfer

A transfer is distinct from **disenrollment** (Section 7.9). Disenrollment — which would end CAP/DA participation entirely — occurs only in specific circumstances such as:
- Loss of Medicaid eligibility
- Physician no longer recommending nursing facility level of care
- Failure to use services for 90 consecutive days
- Inability to ensure health, safety, and well-being through a service plan

3. **Provider Capacity and Capabilities** — Sufficient HCBS providers exist and can effectively serve beneficiaries.
4. **Participant Safeguards** — Beneficiaries are safe and secure, accounting for their informed choices.

# Home Modifications Under CAP/DA (Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2)

> **Source:** NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2 — *Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)*
> **Amendment Status:** No amendments found in the knowledge graph; verify with DHHS for the most current version.

---

## 1. Purpose of Home Modifications

Under **Section 3.4.5** of Policy 3K-2, Equipment, Modification, and Technology services must be designed to:

- **Improve, maximize, or enhance** the CAP/DA beneficiary's mobility, safety, and independence;
- **Improve integration** into the community;
- **Improve environmental and community accessibility**; or
- **Address 24-hours a day, 7 days a week** coverage concerns for the beneficiary.

---

## 2. Where Modifications May Be Made

Per the **Equipment, Modification and Technology** section (`sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:_s275`), covered modifications may be made to:

**Residences:**
- A **primary private residence** owned by the beneficiary or their family;
- A **rented residence**, when the modifications are **portable**; or
- A **rented residence**, when portable modifications are **allowed by the owner**.

**Vehicles:**
- A **primary vehicle** of the CAP/DA beneficiary; or
- A **primary vehicle** of the documented legal guardian or primary caregiver.

---

## 3. Covered Home Modification Items

The policy provides an extensive list of covered modifications, including:

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Ramps & Safety** | Installation, maintenance, and repairs of ramps; grab bars; safety rails and handrails; non-skid surfaces |
| **Accessibility** | Widening of doorways/passages for wheelchair or walker access; door handle replacements; door modifications |
| **Bathroom** | Modification of bathroom facilities (toilet, shower/tub, sink fixtures, water faucet controls, floor urinal adaptations, plumbing, turnaround space) |
| **Bedroom** | Modifications to accommodate hospital beds and wheelchairs |
| **Kitchen** | Modifications to improve accessibility (cabinets, sink fixtures, water faucet controls, plumbing, turnaround space) |
| **Flooring** | Floor coverings for ease of ambulation |
| **Lifts** | Hydraulic, manual, or electronic lifts (including portable lifts used primarily inside the home); lift chairs (when prescribed by a physician and confirmed by a PT or OT) |
| **Emergency Egress** | When medically necessary due to physical limitations of the responsible party |
| **Air Filtration** | Hypoallergenic filters; portable or whole-house air filtration systems (under specific qualifying conditions for severe allergies/asthma or susceptibility to infection) |
| **Smart Home Devices** | Smart bulbs, TV controllers, switches, entryways, clocks, thermostats — **only when** the beneficiary lives alone and the need is identified in the assessment and listed in the person-centered service plan |
| **Backup Generator** | Portable backup generator for a ventilator, when the beneficiary uses the ventilator more than 8 hours/day and would require hospitalization without it during a power outage |
| **Environmental Control Units (ECU/EADL)** | Devices allowing control of electricity-operated aspects of the environment (lights, door openers, HVAC, TV, telephone, hospital bed, computer, small appliances) |
| **Replacement** | Fixtures, mirrors, and storage space removed or damaged during an approved modification |

**Also covered as part of modifications:**
- Technical assistance in device selection
- Training in device use by a qualified assistive technology professional
- Purchase, necessary permits and inspections, taxes, and delivery charges
- Installation
- Assessment of modification by the case manager and applicable inspectors
- Repair of equipment (when repair cost does not exceed cost of new equipment and not covered by warranty — the beneficiary or family must own the equipment)

---

## 4. Exclusions — What Is NOT Covered

The **Limits, Amount and Frequency** section (`sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:_s276`) explicitly excludes:

- Tub replacement
- Portable generators *(except the ventilator backup generator described above)*
- **Addition of square footage** to the home
- **Home renovations**
- Modifications in a dwelling where the owner refuses portable modification
- Non-portable modifications in a rented residence
- Purchase of locks
- Modifications during **new construction**
- Roof repair or replacement
- **Central air conditioning**
- Swimming pools, hot tubs, spas, saunas
- Items of general utility to a non-disabled beneficiary
- Replacement of equipment that has been improperly used, lost, or purposely damaged
- Computer desks or other furniture
- Items that are recreational in nature

---

## 5. Multidisciplinary Team (MDT) Documentation Requirements

Under **Section 5.9.1 — Equipment, Modification, Technology and Supplies** (`sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:5.9.1`), the MDT must provide the following documentation for any home modification request:

1. ✅ **MDT Recommendation** — A recommendation identifying the beneficiary's specific need(s) regarding the assistive technology, equipment, or home modification being requested. **The recommendation must state the cost of the item required.**

2. ✅ **Training Plan** — A plan for how the beneficiary and family will be trained on the use of the equipment. Training must be:
   - Documented by the case manager as **completed**, and
   - **Signed** by the CAP/DA beneficiary or responsible party.

3. ✅ **Statement of Need** — A statement of need identified in the **person-centered service plan**.

4. ✅ **Evidence of Medical Need** — Evidence of medical need recommended by the MDT or by a **physician**, when applicable.

5. ✅ **Itemized Shipping Costs** — Shipping costs itemized in the proposal request.

6. ✅ **Other Item-Specific Information** — Any other information required for the specific equipment requested.

7. ✅ **Quotes** — When quotes are required for purchase, adaptation, or modification, **NC Medicaid determines how many quotes are required**.

8. ✅ **Special Circumstances** — NC Medicaid or its designee determines the appropriate professional(s) to make written recommendations when special circumstances are presented.

---

## 6. Comprehensive Multidisciplinary Needs Assessment

The MDT's work is grounded in the **CAP Comprehensive Multidisciplinary Needs Assessment** (Section 5.4), which must address all of the following domains:

- Contact information
- Diagnosis and History
- Medications and Precautions
- Skin; Neurological; Sensory and Communication; Pain; Musculoskeletal; Cardio-Respiratory; Nutritional; Elimination
- Mental Health
- Informal Support
- Housing and Finances
- Provider Agencies
- Other Planning Considerations

The **Initial Multidisciplinary Comprehensive Assessment** (Section 5.4.1) must:
- Address all aspects of the applicant's risk factors (medical, physical, functional, psychosocial, behavioral, financial, social, cultural, environmental, legal, vocational, educational, and other areas);
- Identify conditions and needs for risk mitigation; and
- Analyze in a multidisciplinary format the current assessment, any previous assessments from other programs, and other pertinent information to determine risk indicators, health and safety concerns, and potential services.

---

## Key Takeaways for Practitioners

> ⚠️ **Rented residences:** Modifications must be portable OR the landlord must provide written permission.
> ⚠️ **Lift chairs** require both a physician prescription AND confirmation by a Physical or Occupational Therapist.
> ⚠️ **Smart home devices** are only covered when the beneficiary lives alone and the need is documented in the assessment and service plan.
> ⚠️ **Air filtration systems** have specific qualifying conditions — all other preventive measures must have been attempted first.
> ⚠️ **Training** on any equipment must be documented as completed and signed by the beneficiary or responsible party.

## NC Medicaid Therapeutic Leave from Nursing Facilities

**Governing Policy:** Clinical Coverage Policy 2B-1, Section 5.8 — *Therapeutic Leave*
*(No amendments on file; policy is current as written.)*

---

### 📅 How Many Days Are Allowed?

- **Up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** — taken from any Medicaid-reimbursed nursing facility bed.
- **No more than 15 consecutive days** may be taken at one time without prior approval from NC Medicaid.
- Leave days **exceeding the 60-day annual limit** will **not** be reimbursed by Medicaid.

---

### ✅ Conditions That Must Be Met

1. **Therapeutic purpose only** — The leave must be taken solely for therapeutic purposes; it cannot be used for receiving inpatient or nursing services at another facility or a different level of care paid for by Medicaid.

2. **Physician order required** — The resident's **attending physician** must order the therapeutic leave.

3. **Documented in the plan of care** — The necessity for leave must be documented in the resident's **plan of care**.

4. **Therapeutic justification in health record** — A written therapeutic justification for **each instance** of leave must be entered into the resident's **health record**.

5. **Bed reservation** — The facility must **hold the resident's bed** during the leave and may not derive any other Medicaid revenue for that resident during the absence (only the bed-hold reimbursement is allowed).

6. **Midnight census notation** — Residents on therapeutic leave must be noted as such on the **facility's midnight census**.

7. **Cumulative record-keeping** — Facilities must maintain a **cumulative record** of therapeutic leave days taken by each resident, and the official record must also be maintained by the State or its agent.

8. **Subject to review** — The therapeutic justification is subject to review by the State or its agent during **scheduled on-site medical reviews**.

---

### 💰 Reimbursement Rules

- Facilities are reimbursed at their **full current Medicaid bed rate** for days a bed is reserved due to therapeutic leave.
- Facilities **bill Medicaid for approved therapeutic leave days as regular residence days**.
- **Ambulance/transportation** to the site of therapeutic leave is **not reimbursed** by Medicaid (it is not considered an emergency transport).

---

### ⚠️ Key Exclusion

Therapeutic leave **does not apply** when the purpose of the leave is to receive **inpatient or nursing services** at another location or a different level of care within the same facility, if those services are paid for by Medicaid.

---

**Source:** NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 2B-1, Section 5.8 — *Therapeutic Leave*. No amendments currently on file. If you are dealing with a specific case, it is advisable to verify current policy with NC DHHS, as policies can be updated.

# Private Duty Nursing: Provider Termination Notification Requirements

NC Medicaid governs PDN termination notifications under **two separate clinical coverage policies** depending on the care setting:
- **Clinical Coverage Policy 3G-1** — PDN provided in the **home**
- **Clinical Coverage Policy 3G-2** — PDN provided in **school settings**

Both policies have been checked for amendments and no change notices have modified these provisions.

---

## 🔔 Notification of Termination (Section 5.2.4.1)

### When the **PDN Service Provider** Discharges the Beneficiary

**Policy 3G-1 (Home):**
- The provider must submit the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)** to NC Medicaid **within 5 business days**.
- If the discharge is because **another source of nursing care coverage** exists, the provider must also notify NC Medicaid within 5 business days and include:
  - The **last date PDN services were provided** and can be billed to Medicaid
  - The **name of the other coverage source**

**Policy 3G-2 (School):**
- The provider must send a copy of the **physician's order to terminate services** to NC Medicaid **within 5 business days**.
- If the discharge is due to **another source of nursing care coverage**, the provider must notify NC Medicaid **in writing**, including:
  - The **last date PDN services were provided** and can be billed to Medicaid
  - The **name of the other coverage source** (as applicable)

---

### When the **Attending Physician** Discharges the Beneficiary

**Policy 3G-1 (Home):**
- The PDN service provider must submit to NC Medicaid **within 5 business days**:
  - The **attending physician's order** to terminate PDN services
  - The **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)**
- ⚠️ **Important:** The decision of the attending physician and/or the PDN service provider to discharge the beneficiary **cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid**.

**Policy 3G-2 (School):**
- The PDN service provider must provide NC Medicaid **within 5 business days**:
  - The **physician's order** to terminate beneficiary services

---

### When Services Are Terminated Due to **Loss of Medicaid Eligibility** or **30-Day Gap in Services**

Both policies (3G-1 and 3G-2) require that if:
- Services are terminated due to the **beneficiary's loss of NC Medicaid eligibility**, OR
- **No PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days** for any reason (including hospitalization)

→ The **prior approval process must be initiated again** from the beginning (per Subsections 5.1 and 5.2 of each policy).

> **Policy 3G-2 adds:** PDN service providers must **notify NC Medicaid when a beneficiary is hospitalized**.

---

### When **NC Medicaid** Initiates Termination

Under **Policy 3G-1**, NC Medicaid may terminate PDN if a review shows that Medicaid eligibility, policy criteria, and/or medical necessity is not met. In that case:
- NC Medicaid (or its designee) must provide **written notice of the adverse decision** to the beneficiary/legal representative
- The notice must include **information about appeal rights**

---

## 📉 Notification of Reduction (Section 5.2.4.2)

If services are **reduced** (rather than fully terminated), similar 5-business-day notification rules apply:

| Scenario | Required Submission (within 5 business days) |
|---|---|
| **Provider** reduces services | Physician's order to reduce + **DMA-3511 (PDN Change Request Form)** (3G-1) / Physician's order (3G-2) |
| **Physician** reduces services | Physician's order to reduce + DMA-3511 (3G-1) / Physician's order (3G-2) |
| **NC Medicaid** initiates reduction | NC Medicaid may request additional info; provider has **10 business days** to respond or NC Medicaid proceeds |

---

## 📋 Summary of Key Requirements

| Requirement | Timeframe |
|---|---|
| Submit discharge summary (DMA-3513) or physician's termination order | **5 business days** |
| Notify NC Medicaid of alternative coverage source | **5 business days** (3G-1) / In writing, no specific deadline stated (3G-2) |
| Respond to NC Medicaid's request for additional information (reduction) | **10 business days** |
| Re-initiate prior approval after 30-day service gap | Before resuming services |

---

## ⚠️ Key Takeaways for Advocates

1. **Provider-initiated discharges are not appealable to NC Medicaid** (Policy 3G-1, Section 5.2.4.1). Beneficiaries cannot challenge the provider's or physician's decision to discharge through NC Medicaid's appeal process.
2. **NC Medicaid-initiated terminations ARE appealable** — written notice with appeal rights must be provided.
3. **Hospitalization triggers re-authorization** if it extends beyond 30 consecutive days without PDN services.
4. School-based PDN (3G-2) has an **additional hospitalization notification requirement** not present in 3G-1.

> **Recommendation:** Given the high stakes of PDN termination, verify current forms (DMA-3513, DMA-3511) and submission procedures directly with NC Medicaid, as form numbers and submission processes can change.

# NC Medicaid: Definition of "Terminally Ill" and Hospice Certification Requirements

## 1. Definition of "Terminally Ill"

NC Medicaid adopts the same standard used under federal Medicare hospice rules. The definition is stated plainly in **DHHS Policy MA-3540, Section B (Restrictions)**:

> *"The physician must certify that the recipient is terminally ill; that is, **in the physician's professional opinion, the recipient has a prognosis of six months or less to live if the disease or illness follows its usual course**."*

This is consistent with the federal standard at **42 CFR § 418.22(b)(1)**, which requires that:

> *"The certification must specify that the individual's prognosis is for a **life expectancy of 6 months or less** if the terminal illness runs its normal course."*

**Key point:** The 6-month prognosis is based on the *normal course* of the illness — it does not mean the patient will necessarily die within 6 months, nor does it disqualify a patient who lives longer than expected. It is a clinical judgment, not a guarantee.

---

## 2. Who Must Certify

### Initial 90-Day Benefit Period
Two certifications are required (**Clinical Policy 3D, Section 5.4.3**; **42 CFR § 418.22(c)(1)**):
1. **The hospice medical director** (or physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group); **AND**
2. **The patient's attending physician**, if the patient has one.

### Subsequent Benefit Periods
Only **one certification** is required — from the **hospice medical director or physician member of the IDG** (Clinical Policy 3D, Section 5.4.3).

### Non-Physician Practitioners
A Medicare-recognized non-physician practitioner (e.g., nurse practitioner) **may conduct the face-to-face encounter** but **is prohibited from certifying terminal illness**. If the patient's attending physician is a non-physician practitioner, the hospice medical director or physician designee must certify (**Clinical Policy 3D, Section [Attestation Statement for Non-Physician Practitioner]**).

---

## 3. What the Certification Must Contain

Per **Clinical Policy 3D, Section D (Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness)** and **42 CFR § 418.22(b)**:

- **A physician narrative** that briefly synthesizes the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis. The narrative must:
  - Reflect the **patient's individual clinical circumstances** (no check-boxes or boilerplate language)
  - Attest that the physician composed it after reviewing the medical record and/or examining the patient
  - Be signed and dated by the certifying physician
- **Benefit period dates** to which the certification applies
- **Supporting clinical documentation** (medical history, clinical notes, assessment tools)

---

## 4. Timing of Certification

Per **Clinical Policy 3D, Section 5.4.1** and **42 CFR § 418.22(a)**:

| Situation | Requirement |
|---|---|
| General rule | Written certification obtained **before** submitting a claim for payment |
| If written cert. not available within 2 days | **Oral certification** within 2 calendar days; written cert. before claim submission |
| Initial certifications | May be prepared **no more than 15 calendar days** before the effective date of election |
| Recertifications | May be prepared **no more than 15 calendar days** before the start of the next benefit period |

---

## 5. Face-to-Face Encounter Requirement

Beginning with the **3rd benefit period** and every period thereafter, a **hospice physician or nurse practitioner must conduct a face-to-face encounter** with the patient (**Clinical Policy 3D, Section 5.4.1**; **42 CFR § 418.22(a)(4)**):

- Must occur **prior to, but no more than 30 calendar days before**, the 3rd benefit period recertification
- The narrative for the 3rd and subsequent recertifications must **explain why the clinical findings of the face-to-face encounter support a life expectancy of 6 months or less**
- Supporting documentation for NC Medicaid prior authorization at this stage includes the **NC Medicaid Hospice Prior Approval Authorization Form (DMA3212)**, Hospice Recertification of Terminal Illness, Physician Plan of Treatment, and clinical assessment tools (e.g., FAST, Palliative Performance Scales, NYHA) (**Clinical Policy 3D, Section 5.2.2.2**)

---

## 6. Patient Election and Waiver

Per **DHHS Policy MA-3540, Section B**:
- The **recipient (or their representative) must sign an election agreement** for Medicaid hospice coverage.
- By electing hospice, the patient **waives Medicaid coverage of certain other services** for treatment of the terminal illness and related conditions.
- Hospice services **do not count toward a recipient's professional services visit limit**.

# Speech Therapy via Telehealth Under NC Medicaid

Speech therapy (speech-language pathology) services may be delivered via telehealth under NC Medicaid, subject to specific conditions and limitations. The rules are governed primarily by **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A** (Outpatient Specialized Therapies) and **Clinical Coverage Policy 10C** (Speech-Language Therapy), with overarching telehealth requirements set by **Clinical Coverage Policy 1H** (Telehealth, Virtual Communications and Remote Patient Monitoring, effective **February 1, 2025**). No amendments have been issued to either Policy 10A or 10C.

---

## 1. When Telehealth Is Medically Necessary

Per **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, Section e. (Telehealth)**, telehealth delivery may be medically necessary when:

- The **beneficiary's medical condition** is such that **exposure to others should be avoided** (e.g., immunocompromised patients); **or**
- The beneficiary's **location is remote or underserved** such that access to appropriately qualified providers is limited.

---

## 2. Core Conditions That Must Be Met

The following criteria **must** be considered before providing speech therapy via telehealth (**Policy 10A, Section e.**):

- **Telehealth must be used as an adjunct to in-person care, not a replacement** — unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable.
- **Telehealth must be in the best interest of the beneficiary** — not used as a convenience for the therapist.
- **Telehealth must never be used solely to increase therapist productivity.**

---

## 3. General Telehealth Requirements (Policy 1H, Section 3.2.1)

Providers must also satisfy these cross-cutting requirements:

- Services can be **safely and effectively delivered** via telehealth.
- The beneficiary's **behavioral, physical, and cognitive abilities** to participate must be considered.
- The **beneficiary's safety** must be carefully assessed for the complexity of services.
- If a **caregiver or facilitator** is needed to assist, their ability and safety must also be considered.
- Services must conform to **professional standards of care**: ethical practice, scope of practice, and applicable federal/state/licensing board rules.
- Providers must **obtain and document verbal or written consent** (or document why consent could not be obtained).
- **Beneficiaries cannot be required to use telehealth** — they must be allowed access to in-person services upon request.
- Providers must **verify the beneficiary's identity** using two points of identification before initiating the session.
- **Beneficiary privacy and confidentiality** must be protected.

# Medical Loss Ratio (MLR) Requirements for Medicaid Managed Care: Federal Law and NC Implementation

## 1. What Is the MLR?

The **Medical Loss Ratio (MLR)** is the percentage of premium/capitation revenue that a managed care organization spends on **actual medical care and quality improvement activities**, as opposed to administrative costs, profits, and overhead. A higher MLR means more dollars go to patient care.

---

## 2. Federal MLR Standard: 85%

### The Core Rule
Under **42 CFR § 438.8(c)**, if a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR for its MCOs, PIHPs (Prepaid Inpatient Health Plans), and PAHPs (Prepaid Ambulatory Health Plans), that minimum **must be at least 85%**. This 85% floor is the same standard used for projecting actuarial soundness under § 438.4(b).

> *"If a State elects to mandate a minimum MLR for its MCOs, PIHPs, or PAHPs, that minimum MLR must be equal to or higher than 85 percent (the standard used for projecting actuarial soundness under § 438.4(b)) and the MLR must be calculated and reported for each MLR reporting year by the MCO, PIHP, or PAHP, consistent with this section."*
> — **42 CFR § 438.8(c)**

### Applicability
The requirement applies to **all MCOs, PIHPs, and PAHPs** under state contracts starting on or after **July 1, 2017**. For multi-year contracts not starting in 2017, the MLR calculation and reporting obligation began with the rating period starting in 2017. *(42 CFR § 438.8(a))*

### CHIP Programs
The same 85% standard applies to CHIP managed care programs. Under **42 CFR § 457.1203(c)**, state payment rates must be designed to reasonably achieve an MLR standard:
- Equal to **at least 85 percent** for the rate year; and
- That provides for **reasonable administrative costs**.

---

## 3. How the MLR Is Calculated

### The Formula (42 CFR § 438.8(d)–(f))
**MLR = Numerator ÷ Denominator**

**Numerator** (what counts as "medical spending") includes:
- **Incurred claims** — direct payments to providers, unpaid claims liabilities, withholds from provider payments, coordination of benefits recoveries, IBNR reserves, contingent benefit reserves, and incentive/bonus payments tied to clinical quality standards
- **Quality improvement expenditures** — activities that improve health care quality
- **Fraud prevention activities**

*Key deductions from incurred claims:* overpayment recoveries from providers and prescription drug rebates received.

**Denominator** (total revenue) includes capitation payments received, minus licensing/regulatory fees and federal/state taxes.

### Credibility Adjustments (42 CFR § 438.8(b))
The federal rule recognizes that small plans may have statistically unreliable experience:
- **Full credibility**: Sufficient experience → no adjustment; plan is measured against the MLR standard
- **Partial credibility**: Sufficient but with statistical uncertainty → a **credibility adjustment** is added to the MLR to account for random variation
- **No credibility**: Insufficient experience → the plan is **not measured against any MLR requirements**

---

## 4. Federal Oversight and Remittance Requirements

### State Reporting to CMS (42 CFR § 438.74(a))
States must **annually submit to CMS** a summary description of each MLR report received from contracted MCOs/PIHPs/PAHPs. The summary must include, at minimum:
- The numerator and denominator amounts
- The MLR percentage achieved
- Number of member months
- Any remittances owed

### Remittance of Federal Share (42 CFR § 438.74(b))
If a state requires an MCO/PIHP/PAHP to pay remittances for failing to meet the minimum MLR, the **state must reimburse CMS for the federal share** of that remittance (accounting for applicable FMAP differences). The state must also submit a separate report describing the methodology used to calculate the state/federal share split.

---

## 5. North Carolina's Implementation

### NC's Assurances in Its State Plan Amendments

# NC Medicaid Coverage of CAR-T Cell Therapy
**Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17 | Effective April 1, 2025 | No amendments on file**

---

## 1. General Medical Necessity Criteria (Section 3.1)
All three of the following must be met:

- The therapy is **individualized, specific, and consistent** with the confirmed diagnosis and not in excess of the beneficiary's needs;
- The therapy can be **safely furnished**, and no equally effective, more conservative, or less costly treatment is available statewide; and
- The therapy is furnished in a manner **not primarily for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.

---

## 2. Specific Coverage Criteria (Section 3.2.1)
All of the following must be satisfied:

1. **FDA Approval**: The CAR T-cell therapy must have received approval from the U.S. FDA.
2. **FDA Guidelines Compliance**: The therapy must be administered per FDA-approved guidelines regarding:
   - Indications and usage
   - Dosage and administration
   - Dosage forms and strengths
   - Warnings and precautions
3. **Certified Treatment Center**: The therapy must be administered at a **certified or authorized treatment center**. If the therapy is subject to a **Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS)** program:
   - The treatment center must be **enrolled in the REMS**; and
   - Providers must be **trained in managing cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurological toxicities**.

---

## 3. What Is NOT Covered (Sections 4.1 & 4.2.1)

### General Exclusions (Section 4.1):
- Beneficiary does not meet eligibility or general coverage criteria
- Service duplicates another provider's service
- Service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**

### Specific Exclusions (Section 4.2.1):
- The CAR T-cell therapy **has not received FDA approval**
- The therapy is administered **outside FDA guidelines** (indications, dosage, forms)
- The therapy requires a REMS program but is administered at a **facility not enrolled** in that REMS
- **Repeat treatment** in beneficiaries who have previously received another CAR T-cell therapy
- The beneficiary's **psychosocial history limits ability to comply** with pre- and post-infusion medical care
- **Current non-compliance** by the beneficiary or caretaker that would make adherence to a disciplined medical regimen improbable

---

## 4. Prior Authorization Documentation Requirements (Section 5.2.2)
The following must be submitted with a prior approval request:

- **Letter of medical necessity** signed by the attending physician documenting:
  - Past chemotherapy regimens and dates
  - Clinical and social history
  - Indications for CAR T-cell therapy
- **Verification of certified/authorized treatment center** status (or a copy of the contract between the facility and the manufacturer)
- **Serologies less than 3 months old**: HIV and Hepatitis panel (positive results may be older than 3 months)
- **All diagnostic and procedure results**, including bone marrow biopsy (not more than 6 months old)
- Other diagnostic tests as appropriate
- **Complete psychological and social evaluation** covering:
  - Beneficiary's medical compliance history
  - Beneficiary's support network
  - Post-treatment care plan (with primary and secondary care providers identified)
  - History of mental health issues, substance use, or legal issues

---

## 5. Provider Certification Requirements (Section 6.2)
Administering hospitals and clinics must:
- Be **specially certified** and have **on-site, immediate access to tocilizumab** (used to treat CRS); and
- Ensure all prescribers, dispensers, and administrators are **trained in managing CRS and neurological toxicities**.

---

## Key Definitions (Section 1.1)
- **Certified/Authorized Treatment Center**: A facility approved to administer CAR T-cell treatments, meeting manufacturer and regulatory requirements, with staff trained in the full CAR T-cell process including adverse effect management.
- **Rescue Transplant**: A stem cell rescue procedure that may be relevant in the context of prior treatment history.

---

## ⚠️ Important Notes
- **No amendments** have been issued to this policy as of the current database.
- The policy does **not** cover repeat CAR T-cell therapy if the beneficiary has previously received a different CAR T-cell product — this is a hard exclusion.
- The psychosocial evaluation is a **mandatory prior authorization document**, not optional — non-compliance history can be grounds for denial.
- Given the high stakes and cost of this therapy, always verify current policy status directly with **NC DHHS DMA** or the NC Medicaid Clinical Policy team before submitting a prior authorization request.

## NC Innovations Waiver: Exceeding the Individual Base Budget

**Short answer: Yes** — a participant can request services that exceed their individual base budget, and the base budget is explicitly *not* a binding cap. Here is the full picture, drawn directly from **Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P (NC Innovations)**, effective November 1, 2016, amended April 1, 2023.

---

### 1. How the Individual Budget Is Set

The individual budget is calculated using the **Supports Intensity Scale (SIS)** assessment — a standardized tool that measures a participant's support needs across domains including home living, community living, employment, health and wellness, social activities, and protection and advocacy. (Policy 8P, Section: *Overview of the SIS Assessment Tool*)

- For beneficiaries **age 16 and older**: the SIS for Adults is used.
- For beneficiaries **age 5–15**: the SIS for Children is used.
*(Policy 8P, Section: "The SIS Assessment in NC Innovations")*

The SIS score drives a **category assignment**, which in turn generates the **base budget** — the starting dollar amount for planning services.

---

### 2. What the Base Budget Covers (and What It Doesn't)

The budget tool has two components:

**Base Budget Services** include:
- Community Networking Services
- Day Supports
- Community Living and Supports
- Respite
- Supported Employment

**Non-Base Budget Services** (not counted against the base budget) include:
- Assistive Technology Equipment and Supplies
- Community Navigator Services
- Community Transition Services
- **Crisis Services**
- Financial Support Services
- Home Modifications
- Individual Goods and Services
- Natural Supports Education
- Specialized Consultation Services
- Vehicle Modifications
- Residential Supports
- Supported Living

*(Policy 8P, Sections: "Base Budget Services are:" and "Non-Base Budget, are:")*

> ⚠️ **Important:** Non-base budget services are authorized separately and do not reduce the base budget amount.

---

### 3. Can a Participant Request Services That Exceed the Base Budget?

**Yes — explicitly.** Policy 8P states directly:

> *"He or she may request services that cost in excess of his or her base budget if he or she believes his or her needs cannot be met within his or her base budget; and*
> *The results of the SIS and the base budget are **guidelines that do not constitute a binding limit** on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized, and if the LME/MCO determines services to be medically necessary, they will be authorized, regardless of the base budget."*

*(Policy 8P, Section: "Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes," sec:doc:clinical_policy:8P:_s564)*

This is a critical protection: **the base budget is a planning guideline, not a hard cap.** If the LME/MCO (your local managed care organization) determines that additional services are **medically necessary**, those services must be authorized even if they exceed the base budget.

---

### 4. What Happens If a Request Is Denied?

The same section requires:

> *"If any request for authorization of services is denied, the LME/MCO will notify the individual of the reasons for the decision and how to appeal."*
> *"How to file a grievance regarding the base budget if he or she wishes to do so."*

*(Policy 8P, Section: "Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes")*

So the participant has **two distinct rights** when services are denied or the budget is disputed:
1. **Appeal** the denial of authorization (with written notice of reasons and appeal instructions).
2. **File a grievance** regarding the base budget itself.

---

### 5. Challenging the Underlying SIS Score

Because the base budget flows from the SIS score, participants who believe their SIS score is too low also have recourse:

- **Within 30 calendar days** of receiving the SIS score, the beneficiary or legally responsible person may contact the LME/MCO with questions or concerns.
- Within **3 business days**, the SIS Interviewer must call to review the summary and answer questions.
- If the participant wants to meet or requests a new SIS, a **face-to-face meeting** must occur within **2 weeks**.
- A new SIS must be scheduled **within 90 days** of the request, conducted by a different SIS Interviewer whenever possible.
- The participant may also **file a grievance** (42 C.F.R. § 438.400; N.C.G.S. § 108D-12).
- **Critically:** *"Failure to grieve a SIS evaluation does not constitute a waiver of the beneficiary's right to challenge the correctness of the SIS evaluation when requesting services or during a service appeal."*

*(Policy 8P, Sections: "Re-assessments and Addendums" and sec:doc:clinical_policy:8P:_s554)*

---

### 6. Special Needs Adjustment

For participants with **time-limited circumstances** requiring higher support, a **Special Needs Adjustment** may be approved:

- Serious injury, illness, or behavioral/mental health crisis requiring additional temporary support → approved for **up to 90 days**, extendable for an additional **90 days**.
- Beneficiary needs a roommate and requires adjustment until one moves in → same 90-day/90-day extension rule.
- Transitioning from a higher level of care (inpatient hospital, ICF/IID) → rate adjustment available.
- Beneficiaries with continued medical or behavioral health needs may be **reassessed for a higher Level** assignment.

*(Policy 8P, Section: "Special Needs Adjustment," sec:doc:clinical_policy:8P:_s521)*

---

### Summary Table

| Situation | What to Do |
|---|---|
| Needs exceed base budget | Request services above the base budget — it is not a binding limit |
| LME/MCO must authorize if medically necessary | Yes — regardless of base budget |
| Authorization denied | LME/MCO must provide written reasons + appeal instructions |
| Disagree with base budget | File a grievance with the LME/MCO |
| SIS score seems too low | Contact LME/MCO within 30 days; request reassessment within 90 days |
| Temporary higher needs | Request a Special Needs Adjustment (up to 90 + 90 days) |

---

### Key Citation
**Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations** (doc:clinical_policy:8P), effective November 1, 2016, amended April 1, 2023. Specifically:
- Section "Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes" (sec:doc:clinical_policy:8P:_s564) — budget non-binding rule and appeal/grievance rights
- Section "Base Budget Services are:" (sec:doc:clinical_policy:8P:_s561) and "Non-Base Budget, are:" (sec:doc:clinical_policy:8P:_s562)
- Section "Special Needs Adjustment" (sec:doc:clinical_policy:8P:_s521)
- Sections "Re-assessments and Addendums" (sec:doc:clinical_policy:8P:_s553–_s554) — SIS challenge rights

> **Recommendation:** If a participant's LME/MCO is treating the base budget as a hard cap and refusing to authorize medically necessary services above it, that is contrary to the explicit language of Policy 8P. The participant should request a written denial, then file both an **appeal** and a **grievance**. Legal aid attorneys should cite Section _s564 directly.

# HIV Case Management Provider Certification Requirements Under NC Medicaid

**Source: Clinical Coverage Policy 12B — Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management**
*(No amendments or change notices currently on file for this document.)*

---

## Part 1: Certification Requirements for HIV Case Management Providers

### A. Agency-Level Requirements (Section 6.2.1)

To become certified as an HIV Case Management provider under NC Medicaid, an agency must:

1. **Track record**: Have a documented, successful record of **at least 3 years** of providing or managing HIV Case Management programs.
2. **Qualified staff**: Ensure that HIV Case Managers (CMs) and supervisors meet the qualifications described in Sections 6.1.1–6.1.5 (see below).
3. **Medicaid enrollment**: Enroll **each physical site** with NC Medicaid as a provider of HIV Case Management services, in accordance with §1902(a)(23) of the Social Security Act.
4. **Legal compliance**: Meet all applicable state and federal laws governing Medicaid provider participation.
5. **Ongoing certification**: Maintain certification and demonstrate compliance with initial and ongoing certification processes.
6. **Quality improvement**: Demonstrate compliance with monitoring and evaluation of case management records through a quality improvement plan.
7. **Records access**: Allow NC Medicaid or a DHHS-designated contractor to review beneficiary records and inspect agency operations and financial records.
8. **Change notification**: Notify NC Medicaid (or DHHS contractor) of proposed changes (e.g., ownership, name, address, phone, dissolution) **within 30 calendar days** of the proposed change, and **no later than 5 business days** of the actual change.
9. **National accreditation**: Within **one year of enrollment**, achieve national accreditation with at least one of the following designated accrediting agencies:
   - Accreditation Commission for Health Care (ACHC)
   - Commission on Accreditation of Rehabilitation Facilities (CARF)
   - Community Health Accreditation Partner (CHAP)
   - Council on Accreditation (COA)
   - Public Health Accreditation Board (PHAB)
   - The Joint Commission
   - Utilization Review Accreditation Commission (URAC)

### B. Administrative Requirements (Section 6.2.1 / Administrative Requirements subsection)

Agencies must also:
- Maintain a **physical business site** (not a private residence or vehicle), verified by a site visit
- Submit an organizational chart, list of owners with ≥5% ownership, and a business plan with financial projections
- Maintain computer capability meeting NC Medicaid IT standards, HIPAA security requirements, electronic billing, and Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT)
- Maintain access to the **NCCCN, Inc.'s web-based applications**
- Complete a **precertification on-site visit**
- Maintain written policies covering: confidentiality, beneficiary grievances, beneficiary rights, non-discrimination, code of ethics, conflict of interest, electronic records, medical records, freedom of choice, transfer/discharge, and abuse/neglect/exploitation identification

### C. Staff Qualification Requirements

#### HIV Case Managers (Section 6.1.1)
A case manager must meet **one** of the following:
- Master's degree in a human services field (social work, sociology, counseling, psychology, nursing, etc.) from an accredited institution
- Bachelor's degree from an accredited school of social work
- Bachelor's degree in a human services field with at least 15 semester hours in social work/counseling/public health **plus 6 months** of social work or counseling experience
- Bachelor's degree in any field **plus 1 year** of counseling or human services experience
- NC licensure as an RN, NP, physician, physician assistant, or certified substance abuse counselor **plus 2 years** of human services experience

#### HIV Case Management Supervisors (Section 6.1.4)
A supervisor must meet **one** of the following:
- Master's degree in a human services field **plus 1 year** of human services experience
- Bachelor's degree from an accredited school of social work **plus 2 years** of human services experience
- Bachelor's degree in a human services field (with ≥15 semester hours in social work/counseling) **plus 2 years** of human services or public health experience
- Bachelor's degree in any field **plus either** 3 years of human services experience, or 2 years of human services experience plus 1 year of supervisory experience
- NC licensure as an RN, NP, physician, physician assistant, or certified substance abuse counselor **plus either** 3 years of human services experience, or 2 years of human services experience plus 1 year of supervisory experience

#### Supervisor Competencies (Section 6.1.5)
Supervisors must also demonstrate the ability to direct and evaluate case management services, apply knowledge of case management principles, conduct analytical evaluations, and apply professional knowledge of federal and state assistance programs for HIV-positive populations.

#### Knowledge, Skills, and Abilities for Case Managers (Section 6.1.3)
CMs must have documented basic knowledge of HIV disease (transmission, treatment, medications, barriers to compliance) within **one year of hire**, plus communication skills, cultural competency, documentation ability, and professional judgment skills.

### D. Training Requirements

- **Initial training** (Section 6.1.7.1): All CMs and supervisors must complete mandatory basic training within **90 days of employment**, covering basic HIV information, scope of work, core case management components, ethics, and documentation requirements.
- **Annual continuing education** (Section 6.1.7.2): **12 hours per year**, including confidentiality, cultural competency, current HIV disease management trends, ethics, and refresher case management content. **At least 6 of the 12 hours must be clinically oriented** (clinical updates).

### E. Recertification (Section 6.2.4)
Providers must periodically recertify by:
- Submitting a complete, signed Recertification Application within **60 calendar days** of receipt
- Submitting updated copies of any changed items from the initial certification
- Submitting copies of all CM and supervisor credentials
- Submitting an annual summary of quality improvement activities and outcome metrics
- Submitting to a **recertification on-site visit**, including review of beneficiary records and other documentation

---

## Part 2: Grounds for Decertification (Section 6.2.5)

NC Medicaid may decertify an HIV Case Management provider for any of the following reasons:

| # | Ground for Decertification |
|---|---------------------------|
| 1 | **Failure to provide core service components** |
| 2 | **Fraudulent billing practices** |
| 3 | **Owner(s) convicted of a felony** |
